title: Applications of Gauss's Law
short_intro: Gauss's law relates the electric flux through any closed Gaussian surface to the net charge enclosed within that surface. It serves as a powerful mathematical tool for evaluating electric fields generated by continuous charge distributions possessing high degrees of spatial symmetry.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Calculation of electric field intensity due to infinite line charge, infinite plane sheet of charge, and uniformly charged spherical shell (inside and outside) using symmetric Gaussian surfaces.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation and analysis of electric field due to solid non-conducting spheres with uniform volume charge density, concentric conducting shells, electrostatic pressure on charged surfaces, and energy density of electrostatic fields.

prerequisites: Definition and calculation of electric flux through a surface
Surface integrals and vector calculus fundamentals

concept_notes.heading: Choice of Gaussian Surface
bullets: A Gaussian surface is an imaginary closed surface chosen to evaluate the electric flux for solving symmetrical electrostatic problems.
The surface must be chosen such that the electric field magnitude E is constant at all points on the surface where flux is calculated.
The angle theta between the electric field vector and the area vector must be either 0 degrees or 90 degrees everywhere on the surface.

concept_notes.heading: Electric Field of an Infinite Line Charge
bullets: For an infinitely long straight wire with uniform linear charge density lambda, the electric field is radially directed outward (or inward if negative).
A coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length l is chosen to exploit cylindrical symmetry.
The electric field varies inversely with distance r from the line charge, independent of the longitudinal coordinate.

concept_notes.heading: Electric Field of an Infinite Plane Sheet of Charge
bullets: For an infinite flat sheet with uniform surface charge density sigma, the electric field is uniform, perpendicular to the sheet, and independent of distance.
A cylindrical or pillbox Gaussian surface penetrating the sheet symmetrically is used for evaluation.
The net flux passes only through the two flat end caps of the pillbox, while the curved side contributes zero flux.

concept_notes.heading: Electric Field of a Uniformly Charged Spherical Shell
bullets: For a thin spherical shell of radius R carrying total charge Q, the electric field outside behaves as if all charge is concentrated at the center.
The electric field inside a uniformly charged hollow spherical shell is identically zero everywhere.
Spherical symmetry dictates that the Gaussian surface must be a concentric sphere of radius r.

derivations.title: Electric Field due to an Infinite Line Charge
derivations.conditions: Infinite length, uniform linear charge density lambda, distance r from the axis
steps: Choose a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length l.
Apply Gauss's law: oint E cdot dA =  rac{q_{	ext{enclosed}}}{varepsilon_0}.
Evaluate the surface integral over the three parts: two flat ends and one curved cylindrical body.
The flux through the flat ends is zero because E is perpendicular to dA. The flux through the curved surface is E(2pi r l).
Equate the total flux to the enclosed charge q_{	ext{enclosed}} = lambda l divided by varepsilon_0.
Simplify to obtain the final expression for electric field magnitude.

derivations.title: Electric Field due to an Infinite Plane Sheet of Charge
derivations.conditions: Infinite planar sheet, uniform surface charge density sigma
steps: Consider a rectangular or cylindrical Gaussian pillbox of cross-sectional area A intersecting the sheet symmetrically.
The electric field is perpendicular to the sheet, pointing outward on both sides.
The flux through the curved side of the pillbox is zero because E is parallel to the surface (E cdot dA = 0).
The flux through the two flat circular ends (each of area A) is EA + EA = 2EA.
The enclosed charge within the pillbox is q_{	ext{enclosed}} = sigma A.
Apply Gauss's law 2EA =  rac{sigma A}{varepsilon_0} and solve for E.

formula_sheet.name: Gauss's Law Integral Form
formula_sheet.equation_html: oint E cdot dA =  rac{q_{	ext{enclosed}}}{varepsilon_0}
formula_sheet.variables: E = Electric field, dA = Area vector element, q_{	ext{enclosed}} = Net enclosed charge, varepsilon_0 = Permittivity of free space
formula_sheet.conditions: Any closed surface in free space or vacuum

formula_sheet.name: Electric Field of Infinite Line Charge
formula_sheet.variables: lambda = Linear charge density, r = Perpendicular distance from axis

formula_sheet.name: Electric Field of Infinite Plane Sheet
formula_sheet.conditions: Near the center of an infinitely large flat sheet

formula_sheet.name: Electric Field of Conducting Plate / Two Sheets
formula_sheet.variables: sigma = Surface charge density on each face
formula_sheet.conditions: Outside a charged conducting plate or between two oppositely charged parallel plates

formula_sheet.name: Electric Field Outside Spherical Shell (r > R)
formula_sheet.variables: Q = Total charge on shell, R = Radius of shell, r = Distance from center

formula_sheet.name: Electric Field Inside Spherical Shell (r < R)
formula_sheet.conditions: r < R (Hollow conducting or non-conducting shell)

formula_sheet.name: Electric Field Inside Solid Non-Conducting Sphere (r < R)
formula_sheet.equation_html: E =  rac{ho r}{3varepsilon_0} =  rac{Qr}{4pi varepsilon_0 R^3}
formula_sheet.variables: rho = Volume charge density, Q = Total charge, R = Radius of sphere
formula_sheet.conditions: Uniform volume charge distribution, r < R

formula_sheet.name: Electrostatic Energy Density
formula_sheet.variables: u = Energy stored per unit volume, E = Electric field magnitude

graphs_and_experiments.title: Electric Field vs Distance for a Spherical Shell
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A graph of E versus r with r on the x-axis and E on the y-axis. E is zero from r = 0 up to r = R, then jumps and drops off as 1/r^2 for r > R.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows discontinuity at the boundary r = R and inverse-square falloff outside the charged shell.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in MCQ matching and graphical identification questions in PGT physics.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Electric Field vs Distance for a Solid Insulating Sphere
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A graph of E versus r where E increases linearly from origin to r = R (E proportional to r), then decreases as 1/r^2 for r > R.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Highlights the difference between volume charge distribution (linear internal field) and surface charge distribution (zero internal field).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in numerical comparison of internal and external field strengths.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Verification of Inverse Square Law conceptually
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Field lines diverging radially from a point charge passing through concentric spherical shells of increasing surface areas.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates conservation of total electric flux regardless of the radius of the chosen spherical Gaussian surface.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual framing for questions on flux independence of surface size.

solved_numericals.question: An infinite line charge produces a field of 9 x 10^4 N/C at a distance of 2 cm. Calculate the linear charge density of the wire.
solution_steps: Identify given values: E = 9 	imes 10^4 N/C, r = 2 cm = 0.02 m.
Use the formula for line charge: E =  rac{lambda}{2pi varepsilon_0 r} =  rac{2klambda}{r}, where k = 9 	imes 10^9 N m^2 / C^2.
Rearrange for lambda: lambda =  rac{E cdot r}{2k} =  rac{9 	imes 10^4 	imes 0.02}{2 	imes 9 	imes 10^9}.
Compute final value: lambda =  rac{1.8 	imes 10^3}{1.8 	imes 10^{10}} = 10^{-7} C/m.

solved_numericals.question: A solid non-conducting sphere of radius R = 5 cm has a total charge Q = 10 microC distributed uniformly throughout its volume. Find the magnitude of the electric field at a point r = 2 cm from the center.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: R = 0.05 m, Q = 10 	imes 10^{-6} C, r = 0.02 m.
Since r < R, use the internal electric field formula for a solid sphere: E =  rac{Q r}{4pi varepsilon_0 R^3}.
Substitute constants and values:  rac{1}{4pi varepsilon_0} = 9 	imes 10^9 N m^2 / C^2.
Compute division: E =  rac{1.8 	imes 10^3}{1.25 	imes 10^{-4}} = 1.44 	imes 10^7 N/C.

solved_numericals.question: Two large, parallel, thin metal sheets carry surface charge densities of +sigma and -sigma respectively, where sigma = 17.7 	imes 10^{-12} C/m^2. What is the electric field intensity in the region between the sheets?
solution_steps: Identify given values: sigma = 17.7 	imes 10^{-12} C/m^2, varepsilon_0 = 8.85 	imes 10^{-12} C^2 / (N m^2).
The electric field due to a single infinite sheet is E =  rac{sigma}{2varepsilon_0}.
Between oppositely charged parallel plates, fields due to both sheets add up constructively in the same direction.
Total field E_{	ext{between}} =  rac{sigma}{2varepsilon_0} +  rac{sigma}{2varepsilon_0} =  rac{sigma}{varepsilon_0}.
Substitute values: E =  rac{17.7 	imes 10^{-12}}{8.85 	imes 10^{-12}} = 2.0 N/C.

assumptions_and_limitations: Gauss's law is universally valid for any closed surface and inverse-square force law, but it is only useful for calculating electric fields when high spatial symmetry (spherical, cylindrical, or planar) allows the electric field magnitude to be factored out of the surface integral.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The term q_{	ext{enclosed}} in Gauss's law includes charges located outside the Gaussian surface.
common_misconceptions.correct: Only charges enclosed strictly within the volume bounded by the Gaussian surface contribute to q_{	ext{enclosed}}.
common_misconceptions.why: External charges contribute to the electric field at the surface, but their net flux contribution through a closed surface is zero.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The electric field on a Gaussian surface is determined solely by the charges inside that surface.
common_misconceptions.correct: The electric field at any point on the Gaussian surface is the vector sum of fields produced by all charges, both inside and outside the surface.
common_misconceptions.why: Although total flux depends only on enclosed charge, individual field vectors depend on the complete charge distribution in space.

quick_revision: Gauss's law equates total electric flux through a closed surface to q_{	ext{enclosed}} / varepsilon_0.
Gauss's Law Integral Form: oint E cdot dA =  rac{q_{	ext{enclosed}}}{varepsilon_0}
Electric Field of Infinite Line Charge: E =  rac{lambda}{2pi varepsilon_0 r}
